scenes.title: Same line — different equation?
body: Goal: change the form, NOT the line
scenes.narration: Can three x plus two y equals fourteen and a completely different-looking equation describe the same line? Yes. Here’s the idea: converting forms is not changing the mathematics. We use legal algebra operations to reveal different information while keeping exactly the same solution points.

scenes.title: What slope-intercept form is showing
body: Common mistake: moving a term without changing its sign
scenes.narration: Slope-intercept form is y equals m x plus b because it exposes the slope and y-intercept immediately. To get there, isolate y. This is where students often mix things up: when a term moves across the equation, it is really being removed by the same operation on both sides. That is why its sign appears to change.

scenes.title: Move the x-term correctly
scenes.narration: Start with three x plus two y equals fourteen. Subtract three x from both sides. The three x cancels on the left, leaving two y equals negative three x plus fourteen. Notice why the negative sign appears: we did not magically move three x; we subtracted three x from both sides.

scenes.title: Divide EVERY term by 2
body: Common mistake: dividing only the constant
scenes.narration: Now divide the entire equation by two. Two y becomes y, negative three x becomes negative three-halves x, and fourteen becomes seven. A very common mistake is dividing only fourteen. Every term must be divided because we are scaling the whole equation by the same factor.

scenes.title: Quick check: did the line stay the same?
scenes.narration: Quick check with the point two comma four. In the original equation, six plus eight equals fourteen. In the new equation, negative three plus seven equals four. The same point satisfies both, confirming the conversion kept the line unchanged. Recap the idea: choose the form that reveals what you need, then apply each algebra operation to the whole equation consistently. The full lesson is available on SUMMIT.
